row.overview: Buckner's north face is a classic alpine ice and snow climb, holding a sustained slope of moderate steepness that comes into the best shape in late spring and early summer. It is a coveted line for climbers wanting a north-side adventure on one of the range's high summits, often approached from Horseshoe Basin.
row.beta: The North Face is 1,300 feet of 40-50 degree snow and ice climbed in approximately 8-13 pitches, most belayed. Work left of any bergschrund, back right to center of lower face and straight up. Upper rock cliffs force several pitches leftward in a rising traverse. Within 200 feet of summit go left around a craggy-looking outcrop at the end of upper cliffs, then back rightward to gain the summit. The face is wind-scoured in places requiring careful assessment of stability. Route quality varies significantly by conditions; some ascents report ice-hard wind-scoured snow while others encounter moderate powder.
row.turnaround: Establish hard turnaround times based on daylight and climbing pace. Summit must be reached by mid-afternoon to allow safe descent in daylight. If halfway up face by noon, consider retreat.
row.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
row.comms: Cell service is absent in Boston Basin and on Boston Glacier. Satellite communicators or personal locator beacons essential for emergency communication. No reliable communication until return to trailhead.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road (FR-15); self-issue wilderness permit required for overnight camping.
waypoints.directions: Cascade River Road (FR-15) runs east from Marblemount to the road-end loop, a couple of miles past the Boston Basin trailhead at mile 21.7, where the usual approach to this face starts; this road-end start is the Sahale Arm way in, which is also the usual way out. The upper road is narrow gravel and holds snow into early summer.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT/Stehekin trail and climb the Sahale Arm climbers' path north toward Sahale Glacier Camp.
waypoints.directions: From the road-end loop the maintained trail switchbacks up through forest, roughly three dozen short zigzags for about 1,500 ft in the first two miles, then breaks out of the trees and contours east across open slopes to the pass at 3.7 miles. Graded and obvious the whole way.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.note: High camp used as the base for the north-side approach; permit required, exposed site with no reliable shelter from weather.
waypoints.directions: Turn north (left) at the pass onto the Sahale Arm path, which switchbacks steeply out of the pass at first. About 0.8 mile up, a signed split sends the right-hand branch down to Doubtful Lake; stay left. Above that the path follows the crest of the arm and steepens near the top, where the tread fades into moraine boulders marked by cairns. Roughly 2.2 miles from the pass.

waypoints.name: Sahale-Boston col
waypoints.note: Skirt the top of Sahale and cross this saddle (a small 2-person bivy exists here) onto exposed third-class choss en route toward Boston Peak.
waypoints.directions: Rope up and work up the Sahale Glacier toward the summit pyramid, bearing right onto the gentlest part of the upper slope, then climb over or skirt the summit block and drop down the far side to the saddle. This is where the standard Boston Basin approach joins, having come up the Quien Sabe Glacier from high camp.

waypoints.name: Boston Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up here — the upper Boston Glacier is described by climbers as viciously crevassed with cracks scattered randomly across the ice.
waypoints.directions: Follow the loose ridge crest toward Boston Peak over a series of rock humps until an easy ledge system breaks off the ridge and leads down to the ice. Below the ledges is steep snow — take it down in the direction of Buckner rather than continuing along the ridge toward Boston.

waypoints.name: North Face bergschrund
waypoints.note: Work left around the bergschrund/moat at the base of the face, then back right to the center of the lower face before starting the ~1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice.
waypoints.directions: Hold a high line across the glacier straight toward the base of the north face rather than losing height into the middle of the basin. Nearer the face, zig-zag around the large crevasses at its toe; getting past the 'schrund itself often takes some scrambling on rock at the edge of the ice. Parties who want a shorter summit day bivy on the glacier around 7,800 ft.

waypoints.name: Buckner Mountain (southwest summit)
waypoints.note: Face climb tops out on the summit ridge just below the true summit; upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse leftward to finish.
waypoints.directions: About 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, typically 8-13 pitches and mostly belayed, though strong parties solo it when the face is in good nick. Climb straight up the centre of the lower face until the upper cliffs cut it off, then take several pitches of rising traverse leftward. Within roughly 200 ft of the top, go left around a craggy outcrop at the end of those cliffs before cutting back right to finish. The face is wind-scoured in places and conditions swing between hard scoured ice and moderate powder, so judge it before committing to climbing unroped.

row.detailed_rack: Ice screws, a few pickets, two tools per climber, and a glacier rescue kit for the approach.
pro_tips: Climb in late spring for the most reliable neve
Start in the dark to top out before the sun warms the face
In lean, late-season conditions the face can bare out to ice, with the upper exit requiring short 5.8-5.9 rock moves for some parties — assess current conditions before committing

row.pro_needs: Snow and ice anchors as conditions dictate; protection is sparse on open snow.
row.approach: Start from the Boston Basin Trailhead (~3,200 ft), about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road from Marblemount (a separate, shorter-drive trailhead than the Cascade Pass TH used for the SW route). The unmaintained climbers' path follows an old, overgrown mining road for about 1 mile to a former mine site, then becomes a steep boot-path through old-growth forest with roughly four creek/stream crossings, emerging above treeline around 5,300 ft into Boston Basin — about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft of gain, typically 3-4 hours. Boston Basin has two designated backcountry camps used as base for this route: low camp (~5,300 ft) and high camp (~6,300-6,400 ft); an NPS permit is required and camping is restricted to these established sites. From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route, roping up for crevasses, and climb toward Sharkfin Col (rather than the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak). Many parties gain the ridge just east of Sharkfin Col, where a natural/fixed sling anchor is commonly used to make a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — down onto the Boston Glacier; multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above. Once on the Boston Glacier (one of the largest glaciers in the lower 48), rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around a bergschrund and large crevasses near the toe of the face, with some rock scrambling to bypass the 'schrund. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself (~7,800 ft) to shorten summit day. From the base, the North Face climbs about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow/ice: work left of the bergschrund, then back right to the center of the lower face and straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse leftward; within about 200 ft of the summit, go left around a craggy rock outcrop, then back right to the top. Competent parties in good nick conditions often solo this face; less experienced or larger parties belay it with pickets/ice screws. Glacier travel, the Sharkfin Col rappel/downclimb, and typical alpine hazards (rockfall, afternoon softening, weather) are the main approach concerns.
row.descent_text: The standard descent does not reverse the North Face — parties continue over the summit and go down Buckner's southwest slopes. From the top, descend gullies, scree, and snow on the fall line to about 7,200 ft, then traverse down and right across Horseshoe Basin on a broad ledge system at 6,200-6,400 ft (passing near the old Davenport Mine) to a snow finger; ascend the snow finger about 100 ft to regain the rounded ridge above the toe of Sahale's south ridge. Scramble roughly 40 ft up short rock steps, then follow paths through heather and rock for about 300 ft along the ridge crest (with the Davenport Glacier in view), before traversing up and left on slabs and snow above the glacier debris to the moraine flats beneath Sahale. From here, parties who arranged a car shuttle can continue over Sahale Arm and out Cascade Pass; most parties who started at Boston Basin instead re-climb Sahale's south ridge back toward Sharkfin Col and reverse the Quien Sabe Glacier approach to Boston Basin and the trailhead — some elect to 'carry over' with full packs and skip returning to a Boston Basin camp entirely. The southwest-slopes portion of the descent itself is a scree/snow walk-off with no rappelling (0 rappels). However, on the return leg back through Sharkfin Col, expect the same technical step encountered on approach: many parties make one short rappel (a single rope length off the natural/fixed sling anchor at the col is sufficient — no multi-pitch rappelling reported) to get back down onto or off the glacier side, while others downclimb it unroped depending on conditions and party comfort; in bad weather/whiteout, at least one party describes rappelling a steep ice gully near a nearby col with pickets as an alternate exit. Treat this Sharkfin Col step, not the summit slopes, as the route's real technical/rappel hazard.
row.bail: Bailing off the face is committing; retreat usually means downclimbing or building snow anchors. Assess conditions before committing above the bergschrund.

pitch_detail.notes: Continuous or simul-climbed snow-ice face above the Boston Glacier bergschrund; the steepest climbing has been reported near a rock outcrop about halfway up and in the final couloir just below the summit.

itinerary.cal: Best conditions are July-September after avalanche danger passes; since this is a point-to-point route between the Boston Basin and Cascade Pass trailheads, plan a car shuttle or hitch for the exit.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day technical traverse (~18-19 mi point-to-point, an estimated ~6,800+ ft of total gain): approach via Boston Basin to a Boston Glacier camp, climb 8-13 pitches of 40-50 degree snow/ice up the North Face, then continue over the summit to a Horseshoe Basin/Sahale camp and exit via Cascade Pass; exceptionally fast parties have linked the whole thing in one very long day, but 3 days with 2 camps is standard.

access.fees: No fee for day use; overnight backcountry permits cost roughly $10/person per night plus a one-time $6 nonrefundable reservation fee, charged only in the summer season (mid-May-early October) — free the rest of the year.
access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the eleven named cross-country zones — Boston Basin, Eldorado, Forbidden, Hidden Lake, Icy, Inspiration, Nooksack, Price, Sulphide Glacier, Torment Basin and Triad — one of which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. Limits include people and stock. Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Wilderness permit required for overnight stays. Sahale Glacier Camp and Cascade Pass camps are among the most in-demand sites in the park; 60% of permits are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (Early-Access lottery in Feb-Mar, general on-sale in spring), and 40% are held for walk-up. Permits must be picked up/activated in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center the day of or day before the trip.
access.closures: Cascade River Road (FR-15) is typically snow-gated in winter and spring and may not open to the trailhead until early-mid summer; it has also suffered repeated storm washouts in recent years (e.g., August 2025). Check the NPS road-conditions page before driving.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the BOSTON BASIN trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward SHARKFIN COL rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the BOSTON GLACIER. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse SOUTH toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.

A second way in reaches the same glacier over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp.
approach_variants.season: Late May through early July for the best face conditions
hazards: A short rappel or a steep no-fall-zone downclimb off Sharkfin Col on crumbly mixed rock — the crux of the approach, and it has to be reversed
A viciously crevassed upper Boston Glacier with cracks scattered randomly across the ice
A bergschrund at the toe of the face that can run its full width, needing rock scrambling to bypass
Wind-scoured ice on some ascents and moderate powder on others — the face's character changes completely with conditions
Cornices on the summit ridge, and rockfall as the day warms
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE BERGSCHRUND AT THE TOE OF THE FACE, ON THE BOSTON GLACIER, AND THE POSITION TEST IS DIRECTIONAL: from the col you traverse SOUTH across the glacier. If you turned north you are heading for Forbidden's north side.

THE ENTRY MOVE IS A ZIG-ZAG AND IT IS THE POSITIVE TEST: WORK CLIMBER'S LEFT OF THE BERGSCHRUND, THEN BACK RIGHT INTO THE CENTRE OF THE LOWER FACE, AND THEN STRAIGHT UP. Left, right, up. A party that crossed the schrund directly and started climbing where it stood has not found the line the face is climbed on.

WHAT YOU ARE CLIMBING CONFIRMS IT: about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, continuous, with no rock pitches. If you are on rock below the summit ridge, you have drifted off the face.

THE FINISH IS THE OTHER COUNTABLE POINT, AND GETTING IT WRONG COSTS TIME AT THE WORST MOMENT: continue straight up until UPPER ROCK CLIFFS force a rising traverse to the LEFT. Then, within about 200 ft of the summit, GO LEFT AROUND A CRAGGY ROCK OUTCROP at the end of those cliffs, and only then back right to the top. Both moves are left. A party that goes right at the cliff band has misread the finish.

AND THE APPROACH ITSELF IS THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THIS PEAK'S OTHER ROUTE: the Southwest Face is reached over Cascade Pass, Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin, on the opposite side of the mountain, and the two share no ground until the summit ridge. IF YOU WALKED PAST AN OLD MINE IN A BASIN AT 7,000 FT, YOU ARE ON THE SOUTHWEST ROUTE.

climbing_route.label: Lower north face snow/ice
climbing_route.notes: About 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice overall. From the base, work left of the bergschrund, then back right into the center of the lower face and straight up. Competent parties in good conditions often solo the face; less experienced or larger parties belay with pickets and ice screws. Rockfall, afternoon softening and weather are the standing hazards.

climbing_route.label: Rising leftward traverse under the upper cliffs
climbing_route.notes: Continue straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse to the left.

climbing_route.label: Summit exit around the rock outcrop
climbing_route.notes: Within about 200 ft of the summit, go left around a craggy rock outcrop, then back right to the top.

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.notes: The comfortable planned camp, roughly 6,300 to 6,400 ft on a sandy flat below a permanent snowfield, about three to four hours from the road. Everything on this route beyond it is committing, because the way onto the Boston Glacier goes over Sharkfin Col and that involves a rappel or a steep downclimb on poor rock that many parties describe as harder than the face itself. Coming back to this camp means reversing it. A lower camp at about 5,300 ft with its own composting toilet is the alternative if the upper sites are full.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks and the permanent snowfield behind camp, reliable through the season
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required. Boston Basin is one of the small number of zones that accepts advance reservations, and composting toilets serve both the upper and lower camp areas.
bivy.capacity: Hardened sites; the zone allows six parties per night and up to twelve people per party

bivy.name: Boston Glacier bivy
bivy.notes: A planned but fully exposed glacier bivy used to shorten summit day, on one of the largest glaciers in the lower 48. You are camping on a crevassed surface, so probe the platform and its surroundings before dropping the rope, and mark the perimeter. There is no shelter, no running water and no ground: everything is melted, and wind or a change in weather has nowhere to be dodged. The serious point is that it sits past Sharkfin Col — retreat from here means reclimbing that col, so committing to this bivy commits you to the route in a way that camping in Boston Basin does not.
bivy.permit: The glacier is its own cross-country zone on the park permit system, capped at six people per party and six parties per night; human waste on snow and glacier terrain has to be packed out in a blue bag
bivy.capacity: Whatever platform you cut; the Boston Glacier cross-country zone allows six parties per night, six people per party

bivy.name: Sahale–Boston col bivy
bivy.notes: A tiny, spectacular perch on the col between Sahale and Boston, used by parties linking this face with other climbs in the basin or descending over Sahale Arm. It is an emergency-sized site, not a camp: there is room for one small tent, and cornices overhang the Davenport side, so probe out from the sleeping platform before settling in and do not wander in the dark. Wind exposure is total.
bivy.capacity: One small two-person tent's worth of flat ground

row.overview: Grotto Mountain (5,618 ft) is a rugged, lightly-visited peak in the Wild Sky Wilderness (Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest), rising east of Baring Mountain above the South Fork Skykomish River near the US-2 communities of Baring and Grotto. There is no maintained trail to the summit. The line described here follows the east ridge through steep timber and heather bands to a craggy, boulder-strewn summit block overlooking US-2 and the Skykomish valley, with views to Baring, Merchant, and Gunn Peaks. Recent (2024-2025) parties have used an alternate approach via Klinger Ridge — the peak's south ridge — reached from Beckler River Road, crossing to a notch just below the summit block; treat this as a variation on the same peak rather than a confirmed identical line. The 2022 Bolt Creek Fire burned the entire south side of Klinger Ridge, leaving standing dead timber, heavier brush regrowth, and altered route-finding that persist years later — expect more sun exposure and less shade than before the fire.
row.beta: There is no trail beyond the Forest Service road-end. Parties describe pushing through huckleberry brush toward talus (a brushy streambed gives easier passage than the surrounding vegetation), then rising traverses across talus and heathered benches past a small basin/tarn around 4,300ft, up toward the ridge crest near 5,400ft. From there the route works up and right along minor ledges to a talus basin below the summit, then a gully to a col between the summit block and a minor knob to its east, finishing with an exposed class 3-4 scramble to the top. Parties note the literal east ridge crest itself does not go as a through-route.
row.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time given the off-trail nature of the route and the lack of shade on burned terrain — afternoon fog or thunderstorm buildup can make an already unmarked descent much harder.
row.permit: Free self-issue Wild Sky Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
row.descent: Retrace the east ridge down to the approach.

waypoints.name: NF-6514-410 road's end
waypoints.note: Park at the end of the spur off Beckler River Road (FS-65)/FS-6514, about 5 miles past the Eagle Lake trailhead fork; no maintained trail beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: Roughly 6.5 miles of gravel and dirt Forest Service road from pavement. The drive-in is variable and worth confirming with the Skykomish Ranger District before committing to it.

waypoints.name: Brushy drainage / streambed
waypoints.note: Route starts by climbing a mossy, brush-choked streambed that is slick when wet; poor footing before the terrain opens.
waypoints.directions: There is no trail from the car; the line goes straight into thick huckleberry toward the talus above. Rather than fighting the brush, drop into the streambed running alongside it, which is much easier going even though the rock underfoot is slick.

waypoints.name: Saddle east of Grotto Lake basin
waypoints.note: Huckleberry-covered saddle where the route angles right off the drainage onto the ridge proper before contouring toward Klinger Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the drainage and the talus beside it up into the rock basin around 4,300 ft. Route-finding is entirely on you here, with no trail and no markers, and morning fog frequently sits in this basin well past sunrise, so carry a track you can navigate to.

waypoints.name: Klinger Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn at the top of the basin below Klinger Ridge; snowmelt-fed and a reliable early-season water source before the final push.

waypoints.name: Klinger Ridge meadow gain
waypoints.note: Meadowy ridge crest reached via a rising talus traverse; fog commonly lingers here into mid-morning, obscuring the correct line.
waypoints.directions: From the tarn and basin below the ridge, make a rising traverse across talus into a gully, then climb a heathered slope beneath a cliff band, which dodges a slide-alder tangle, to reach the open meadow crest above 4,600 ft. A cairn near here has pulled parties off the direct line; staying in the gully to about 4,800 ft is the more direct way.

waypoints.name: Notch below summit tower
waypoints.note: Steep talus leads to a notch west of a prominent rock tower; a short vertical downclimb on the south side is exposed and helmet-recommended.
waypoints.directions: Follow the meadow and boulder crest upward, but do not try to hold the literal east ridge crest, which cliffs out and does not go as a through-route. From about 4,800 ft, weave up through steep granite blocks and cross a final talus field to reach the notch.

waypoints.name: Grotto Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Class 4 scramble up a final gully off the notch gains the summit block; views south into the Bolt Creek Fire-burned drainage and across to Mount Baring.
waypoints.directions: Downclimb the short, steep, near-vertical step on the south side of the notch. This is the most exposed move on the route and the rock is loose in places. Then move a short way west into the gully below the summit block and scramble Class 3-4 to the top.

what_to_bring: map/compass or GPS track — no trail or signage on route

pro_tips: Start early to beat summer valley fog and give yourself daylight margin on an unmarked, off-trail scramble.
Carry more water than a typical shaded Cascades scramble — burned terrain on the south side offers little shade.
Summit views take in Baring, Merchant, and Gunn Peaks across the Skykomish valley.
watch_out: No maintained trail — this is off-trail scrambling with real route-finding demands.
2022 Bolt Creek Fire burned the south side of Klinger Ridge: expect standing dead snags, possible debris flows, and heavier brush regrowth.
Morning fog in the Skykomish valley can obscure the route until it burns off later in the day.
row.pro_needs: Most parties scramble this unroped and there is no fixed protection, but the Class 4 moves at the summit have been protected with a short rope, a few slings and a couple of small cams. A helmet is strongly advised for rockfall on the loose talus and in the gully/col below the summit block.
row.approach: Grotto Mountain (5,618') sits east of the more famous Baring Mountain, above the South Fork Skykomish River near the Wild Sky Wilderness boundary. The drive-in is variable and should be reconfirmed with the Skykomish Ranger District, but the trailhead itself is the end of FS spur NF-6514-410, off Beckler River Road (FR-65) — roughly 6.5 miles of gravel/dirt FS road from pavement, ending at a small pullout at about 3,480 ft. There is no maintained trail from here; this is an off-trail scramble the entire way (about 2.4 miles/3,900 ft one-way to the 5,618 ft high point). From road's end, the line immediately enters dense huckleberry brush heading toward talus — a brushy, moss-lined streambed just to the side of the huckleberry slope offers noticeably easier (if slick when wet) passage and is the preferred line reported by recent parties. Follow this drainage/talus combination up into a rock basin around 4,300 ft, where the route makes a rising traverse across talus into a gully, then climbs a heathered slope below a cliff band to avoid a slide-alder tangle. This gains Klinger Ridge at roughly 4,600 ft — open meadow and boulder terrain with pikas and clear views back to Baring Mountain. Continue along/near the ridge crest toward the east summit; from about 4,800 ft below the summit, weave through steep granite blocks and a final talus traverse to a notch just west of a prominent rock tower, then downclimb a short, steep/near-vertical step (exposed, loose in places — helmet warranted) to gain the south side and the true summit. Water is generally abundant from snowmelt streams in the lower basin (below ~4,300 ft) but can dry up by late summer; carry what you need for the upper mountain. Key hazards: thick brush and slick moss low down, sustained off-trail route-finding (fog/whiteout is a real risk with no trail to follow), loose rock and a burn-scarred south-facing slope on Klinger Ridge from the 2022 Bolt Creek Fire, and exposed granite/talus near the summit notch.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or commonly used on this route. Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the steep step back through the summit notch, reverse the granite-block and talus traverse back to about 4,800 ft, then follow Klinger Ridge's meadow/boulder terrain back down. Because the true east ridge crest was found to cliff out / not reasonably traverse in recent trip reports, most parties drop off the ridge into the small basin/tarn area below Klinger Ridge rather than trying to hold the crest, then pick up the ascent streambed line back to the 4,300 ft rock basin. From there, reverse the talus-and-streambed line down through the heathered slope and huckleberry brush to road's end at 3,480 ft, favoring the mossy streambed over bashing straight through brush (watch footing on wet moss). No technical rope work has been reported on this route; a short handline could be a reasonable option for less-confident parties at the summit notch step, but it is a downclimb, not a rappel. Primary hazards on the way down are the same as the approach in reverse — brush, slick streambed rock, and route-finding in fog on a trail-less, partly fire-scarred mountainside — plus the general scramble hazard of downclimbing loose granite steps.
row.bail: If you need to bail, retreat via the ridge crest back toward the drainage/road rather than cutting down through the burned, brushy south-facing slopes off-route, where footing is unstable and visibility is poor.

itinerary.cal: Best attempted July-September once brush has dried out and snow has cleared from the upper talus and summit gully.

days.note: From the Eagle Creek/Beckler River road-end, climbers push through huckleberry brush to a streambed, cross talus around 4,000 ft, then work up heathered slopes and granite steps to a talus basin below the summit block. Since the true east ridge crest is unsuitable for direct travel, most parties detour through the basin and scramble the class 3-4 col from the north ridge to reach the top; morning fog often lingers into mid-morning.

approach_variants.name: Spur road end to Klinger Ridge
approach_variants.notes: There is no trail from the car. The line goes straight into thick huckleberry toward the talus above, but the mossy streambed running alongside that brush is far easier travel even though the rock underfoot is slick. Follow the drainage and its talus up into a rock basin around 4,300 ft, then make a rising traverse across talus into a gully and climb a heathered slope beneath a cliff band, which dodges a slide-alder tangle, onto the open meadow crest above 4,600 ft. Fog sits in the lower basin well past sunrise, and there are no markers to steer by.
hazards: Slick moss in the lower streambed
Standing dead timber and heavy regrowth across the burned south side of Klinger Ridge
Morning valley fog on ground with no trail to follow
Loose, exposed granite at the summit notch

approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts at a notch just WEST of a prominent standing rock tower at about 5,300 ft, and the way to it is not the obvious one. Do not try to hold the literal east ridge crest — it cliffs out and does not go through as a route. From roughly 4,800 ft weave up through steep granite blocks and cross a final talus field to the notch, which is the gap immediately beside the one unmistakable tower on that stretch of crest. There is a decoy lower down: a single cairn near the meadow crest around 4,600 ft pulls parties off the direct line, and staying in the gully to about 4,800 ft is the straighter way. The move that confirms you are at the base is a DOWNclimb rather than a climb — a short, steep, near-vertical step drops off the south side of the notch, loose in places and the most exposed ground on the route, and only once you are through it does the gully below the summit block open up for the final class 3-4 scramble to the top.

bivy.name: Beckler River Campground
bivy.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. This is the natural base for the eastern end of the zone: the same road, continuing north and then west onto FR 6510 and FR 6514, is what gets you to Eagle Rock, to the road end at roughly 3,500 ft used for Grotto Mountain, and to the gentle back-door approach to Eagle Lake. If the campground is full or closed for the season, the upper Beckler road corridor and its spurs are national forest land where dispersed camping is allowed with no permit — the standing rules are to camp at least 100 ft from water, use an existing pullout rather than making a new clearing, stay a maximum of fourteen days in one spot, and obey whatever fire restriction is current. Those spurs are rough, gated in places, and can be locked without warning, so check the gate on your way in rather than discovering it on your way out. Being a valley campground it says nothing about conditions up high; expect snow on the FR 6514 spurs well into spring.
bivy.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
bivy.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.

row.overview: Hibox Mountain (6,548 ft) is the high point of Box Ridge, a rugged sub-ridge of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness about 5 miles east of Snoqualmie Pass, rising above the popular Rachel Lake basin. It's one of the most-climbed scrambles near I-90, combining an easy trail approach with a steep, loose Class 2-3 boot path up Box Ridge and a short, exposed Class 3 summit block. Summit views take in Rampart Ridge, Alta Mountain, Three Queens, Mount Thompson, Rachel Lake, and the Stuart Range.
row.beta: From the Rachel Lake trailhead, follow the maintained Rachel Lake Trail for roughly 2 miles to the first avalanche-chute clearing. A boot path for Hibox leaves the main trail here (or at the second chute crossing) and climbs steeply but stays class 2 through timber to near treeline. Above the trees, go right around the first band of cliffs, then left around a rock outcrop, continue through more timber to a second cliff band, and take the gully on the right to gain the upper mountain. From there head right (east) along the south side of the summit rocks to a gully on the east side, which is climbed with a bit of class 3 near the top to reach the summit. Route-finding is the main challenge; there is no continuous trail above the boot path.
row.turnaround: Turn around at the summit block if exposure feels beyond your comfort.
row.rappels: None; the route is down-climbed via the same line as the ascent.
row.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
row.descent: Reverse the boot path down Box Ridge to Rachel Lake, then out the Rachel Lake Trail to the trailhead.

pro_tips: Bring a helmet for the whole talus/boot-path section, not just the summit block — rockfall from parties above is a known hazard

If you lose the boot path near the avalanche clearings past Rachel Lake, backtrack rather than bushwhacking blind — the real trail reappears under tree canopy a short distance past the obvious false path
Keep climber's right of the gully below the summit block on both ascent and descent; it cliffs out at Class 4 and is a frequent source of epics
watch_out: The correct boot path junction beyond Rachel Lake is easy to miss — a false trail through brush appears first; keep going until you're back under tree canopy to find the real path

row.best_season: July through early October; snow can linger in the upper gully and basin into July in heavy-snowpack years
row.approach: Start at the Rachel Lake Trailhead (Trail #1313, elev. ~2,800 ft) at the end of Box Canyon Road/FR-4930. Follow the Rachel Lake Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the Box Canyon Creek drainage — the grade is easy and well-graded here, mostly Class 1 hiking. At roughly 2–2.2 miles and about 450–500 ft of gain (~3,300 ft elevation), the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing where Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast; this clearing is the key landmark. Just past it (some parties note it's after the second such clearing), watch on the right/climber's-right side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path (the 'Hibox climbers' path') leaving the maintained trail and heading northeast/uphill into the forest — it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. From here the character changes completely: the bootpath climbs steeply (mostly Class 2, with fallen timber to step over) for about 500 vertical feet before breaking out of the trees near a band of cliffs around 5,300 ft. Stay right of this first rock band, then work left around a rock outcrop, continuing through patchy timber to a second, higher cliff band; a gully on the right provides passage through it. Above this the trail opens into a large sloping subalpine meadow (wildflowers in season) that funnels into a loose talus/scree slope — this is the most tedious and slip-prone section of the route, so careful foot placement matters more than pace. A thready boot path threads up through the talus to the south side of the summit block. There is no reliable water past the lower forest/creek section, so carry what you need from the car or treat water low on the mountain. The route-finding through the two cliff bands and the avalanche-path junction low on the trail are the two spots parties most often go astray; a GPS track or recent trip report beta is worth having.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than glissading the scree, which is loose and eroded. From the summit, downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the south side of the summit block (good rock, low exposure, easy Class 3 moves), then pick your way back down through the loose talus/scree field to the sloping meadow. Some parties descend via a slightly different line on the east side of the summit block/east ridge before rejoining the ascent boot path lower down — functionally the same route, just avoid cutting new paths through the scree to limit erosion. Continue down through the two cliff bands (reversing right/left as on the way up) and back into the timber, staying alert for the boot path's exit point onto the maintained Rachel Lake Trail near the ~3,300 ft avalanche clearing — it's easy to miss in the trees when descending. Once back on Rachel Lake Trail #1313, it's an easy, well-graded 2+ miles back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required — the summit block's only technical move is a short, low-exposure Class 3 downclimb, not a rappel. Watch the weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in this range and parties often report hurrying off the loose upper slopes ahead of incoming storms.
row.bail: Reverse the boot path down Box Ridge to the Rachel Lake Trail and walk out the trail to the trailhead.

approach_variants.name: Rachel Lake Trail to the avalanche clearing, then the Hibox climbers' path over two cliff bands
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Rachel Lake trailhead, Trail #1313, about 2,800 ft, at the end of Box Canyon Road / FR-4930. The trail climbs gently through forest along Box Canyon Creek, easy class 1 walking.

At roughly 2 to 2.2 miles and about 3,300 ft the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing. That clearing is the key landmark, because Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast from it.

Above the boot path the tread climbs steeply, mostly class 2 with fallen timber, about 500 vertical feet to a band of cliffs near 5,300 ft. Stay RIGHT of that first band, then work LEFT around a rock outcrop, continue through patchy timber to a SECOND, higher cliff band, and take the gully on the RIGHT through it. Above, a large sloping subalpine meadow funnels into loose talus and scree.

No reliable water past the lower forest. About 5.6 km and 3,900 ft.
hazards: An unsigned, easy-to-lose boot path through brushy avalanche clearings, especially confusing in fog and on descent
A deceptive gully on the southwest side of the summit block that cliffs out at class 4 — stay climbers' right of it
Loose talus and scree above about 4,600 ft with real rockfall risk onto parties below
An exposed class 3 notch and chimney on the summit block, whose downclimb is the part to think about before committing
Lingering snow and ice in the upper gully and basin into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLEARING IS THE FIRST TEST AND THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS ITS PROOF. At roughly 2 to 2.2 miles the maintained trail crosses a brushy avalanche clearing, and from it Hibox's summit block is visible on the ridge to the NORTHEAST. Just past that clearing — some parties say after the SECOND such clearing — watch the RIGHT, climbers'-right, side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path heading northeast and uphill into the forest. It is easy to walk past if you are not looking.

THE TWO CLIFF BANDS ARE A COUNTED SEQUENCE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WANT IN FOG: first band, pass it on the RIGHT; then LEFT around a rock outcrop; second band, take the gully on the RIGHT. Two bands, right then left then right. If you have passed only one band you are not yet on the upper mountain.

AND HERE IS THE WRONG-TURN TRAP THAT MATTERS MOST, at the top: the talus tops out on the SOUTH side of the summit block, and the rock straight above you there is steeper and more broken than it looks. That is the spot where parties commit to the wrong line, and there is a deceptive gully on the SOUTHWEST side of the block that cliffs out at class 4. Do not climb what is above you.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL BASE FINDING: work RIGHT, staying along the south side of the rock and heading EAST, on loose talus over a sloping bed, until a reasonable gully opens on the EAST side of the block. That east gully is the route. It stays easy until the top, where a short NOTCH or narrow chimney gives a bit of genuine class 3 on good, solid holds to a small summit platform.

AND A DESCENT NOTE THAT BELONGS WITH THE FINDING: the boot path through the brushy avalanche clearings is easy to lose on the way down, especially in fog. Look back at the junction on the way up.

climbing_route.label: South side of the summit block
climbing_route.notes: The talus slope tops out on the south side of the summit block. Do not try to climb the rock straight above you here — the direct south side is steeper and more broken than it looks, and it is the spot where parties commit to the wrong line. Instead line yourself up with the south side of the block and prepare to traverse.

climbing_route.label: Traverse east under the block
climbing_route.notes: Work right, staying along the south side of the rock and heading east, until a reasonable gully opens on the east side. The traverse is on loose talus and scree over a sloping bed — the most slip-prone ground on the route, where deliberate foot placement matters more than speed. It is also the last place to turn around easily.

climbing_route.label: East gully and summit notch
climbing_route.notes: Ascend the gully on the east side of the block. It stays easy until the top, where a short notch or narrow chimney runs up to the summit rock and gives a bit of genuine Class 3 scrambling. The rock here is reported as good and the holds solid, but the position is exposed and the summit itself is a small platform with steep ground on several sides. The downclimb of this last step is the part to think about before committing to it, and wet or icy rock changes the character of the notch entirely.

bivy.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
bivy.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
bivy.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

bivy.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
bivy.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.

bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
bivy.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

row.overview: A rugged, three-summited peak (south summit is highest) in the southeastern Olympics within the Mount Skokomish Wilderness, straddling the Olympic National Park boundary near Mount Stone. Built of rotten Eocene pillow basalt, it is reached by a tough, largely off-trail approach and a loose Class 2-3 scramble to the broad summit block. The standard Putvin approach was never inside the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire closure; the Mildred Lakes trail reopened in July 2026, while the Flapjack Lakes side beyond the Staircase developed area stays closed for repairs.
row.beta: From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road, the Putvin Trail climbs about 3,400 ft in roughly 3.5 miles to Lake of the Angels, including a very steep, sometimes near-vertical headwall requiring hand-and-foot scrambling on roots and rock. Beyond the lake, skirt the north/west shore and climb alpine slopes and a scree-and-snow gully (climber's-right gully) to a roughly 5,800 ft saddle at the peak's northeast/east side. From the saddle, cross scree, grass, and rock slopes southwest and scramble the southeast slope/south ridge on generally rotten, loose rock (Class 2, locally 3 to 3+) to the summit. The route has three summit horns; parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true (south) high point. Snow lingers on the gully and saddle well into summer and is reported as firm/frail, so an ice axe is commonly carried into July.
row.turnaround: Set a hard turnaround time before starting based on your pace on the steep Putvin Trail and the current snow/ice state of the saddle gully — the descent is long and exposed to loose rock and heat, and losing daylight on the headwall or ridge significantly raises the risk of a fall.
row.rock_grade: Class 2-3 (unroped scramble; exposed Class 3 ridge crest near the summit)
row.descent: Reverse the route, carefully down-climbing the Class 3 summit section and descending the gullies/snow back toward camp.

row.approach: The standard-route trailhead is the Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of Hwy 101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft elevation. Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels, not Mildred or Flapjack Lakes - those serve neighboring Mount Cruiser/Mount Lena out of the North Fork Skokomish/Staircase side. From the trailhead, Putvin Trail #813 is unmaintained for its last ~1.6 miles but well-traveled and easy to follow when snow-free; the tread is notably steep and narrow with unstable footing in spots as it climbs through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles in, the trail breaks into the open, grassy Whitehorse Creek basin and continues up to Lake of the Angels (about 3.5 miles and roughly 3,400 ft of gain from the trailhead, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace), a scenic alpine lake sitting in a cirque below Mount Stone and the Skokomish massif - this is the last reliable water source and the standard camp for an overnight trip. From the lake, climb westerly up pleasant alpine/heather slopes to a broad 5,800-ft saddle at the northeastern end of Mount Skokomish. From the saddle, a boot path/way-trail contours south and southwest across scree, grass, and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn, before turning to climb the final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge. Total round-trip stats commonly cited are roughly 9-12 miles and about 5,000-5,100 ft of gain, with climbing parties reporting 3.5-5 hours up. Hazards: the narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread; lingering steep snow and real avalanche exposure on the upper slopes well into summer (reports note hazard even in August/September); and notoriously rotten 'Olympic choss' rock and loose scree/talus on the upper mountain and summit block, which is the crux of the route more than any single technical move.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the summit scree/rock to the saddle, then back along the boot path traverse across scree/grass/rock benches around the south and east flanks to the 5,800-ft saddle above Lake of the Angels, down to the lake, and out the Putvin Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - there is no rappelling anywhere on the standard scramble route. The main descent hazard is the same rotten rock and loose scree that makes the ascent tricky: downclimbing the exposed class 3 sections near the summit ridge crest is generally regarded as harder and more hazard-prone than climbing them, and parties should stay well left/south of the steeper cliffy drop-off noted on the north side of the upper mountain (parties specifically warn that contouring too far right/north near the ridge crest 'gets sketchy, exposed, and dangerous' and to cut west over the ridge instead). Watch for rockfall onto climbers below on the scree/talus sections, expect residual snow in the gullies and on the traverse into early summer (ice axe/crampons may be warranted), and budget real time for careful downclimbing rather than assuming a fast glissade-style descent - one party logged about 2.5 hours from summit back to the trailhead, but that was in good, snow-free conditions.
row.bail: Retreat by reversing the route; bail from the approach basins if weather or snow conditions are poor.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the Mildred Lakes trailhead; no pass or fee is needed to park at the Putvin trailhead. Entering via Staircase/Olympic NP requires the $30 park entrance fee (7-day private-vehicle pass; $15 for a walk-in/bike individual pass) or an interagency pass, plus an $8 per person per night backcountry camping fee (booked via Recreation.gov) for Flapjack Lakes.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Standard Wilderness regulations apply (no bikes/motorized use, max group size limits, camp 200 ft from water). Mountain goats are frequently encountered around the peak's base and Lake of the Angels basin — do not approach or feed them; give them a wide berth as they can be aggressive toward hikers seeking salt.
access.permit: No wilderness permit is required for day trips on Olympic National Forest land (Mildred Lakes, Putvin Trail). Camping at Lake of the Angels, which lies inside Olympic National Park, requires an Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit. If approaching via Flapjack Lakes inside Olympic National Park, an overnight wilderness camping permit is required, reservable on Recreation.gov for the Flapjack Lakes zone (bookable mid-April, camping dates mid-June through mid-October); contact the Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100.

Still CLOSED pending hazard-tree removal and infrastructure repair: wilderness trails beyond the developed Staircase area, including the North Fork Skokomish River Trail (from the Staircase Rapids Loop to Home Sweet Home) and the Flapjack Lakes Trail, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026, plus FS-2451 and the Copper Creek Trail (Olympic National Forest alert updated July 8, 2026). approach_variants.notes: THIS IS THE STANDARD APPROACH AND THE ROUTE'S WAYPOINT LIST DESCRIBES A DIFFERENT ONE. Published and trip-report accounts are consistent that Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via the Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAND AT LAKE OF THE ANGELS AND THE CIRQUE ITSELF TELLS YOU WHICH WAY TO GO: MOUNT STONE IS ON YOUR RIGHT, ANOTHER PEAK IS ON YOUR LEFT, AND MOUNT SKOKOMISH IS STRAIGHT AHEAD. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

THE TURN IS AROUND THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE LAKE, on a way trail heading WEST to the ridge. Then take a broad gully SOUTHWEST and up toward the SADDLE JUST NORTH OF POINT 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud, which is why it is quoted here rather than a description of the terrain.

SECOND TEST, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours SOUTH and SOUTHWEST across scree, grass and rock benches around the EAST and SOUTH flanks of the peak, PASSING A LARGE TARN. The tarn is the confirmation. TURN RIGHT AND START CLIMBING WHEN YOU ARE ABOVE THE LARGE TARN — that is the published trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

THIRD TEST, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around LEFT to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has THREE SUMMIT HORNS and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

EXPLICIT WARNING FROM A TRIP REPORT, and it is directional: contouring too far RIGHT (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut WEST over the ridge instead.

approach_variants.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
approach_variants.notes: RECORDED BECAUSE THE ROUTE'S OWN WAYPOINTS DESCRIBE THIS APPROACH, not because it is the standard one. It is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford HUCKLEBERRY CREEK at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot ROOT AND ROCK LADDERS, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail. Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — in the Bear Gulch Fire closure area
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE ON THIS SIDE IS THE OPEN BASIN AND SADDLE BENEATH THE SOUTH PEAK AT ABOUT 5,500 FT, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS UNDERFOOT: THE FOOTING TURNS TO LOOSE, ROTTEN ROCK FROM THERE UP. Below the saddle you are fighting brush and heather; at and above it you are on scree and shattered rock. That transition is the arrival cue and it does not require seeing anything. THE TEST FOR THE APPROACH ITSELF IS THE ROOT LADDER, because it is the one unmistakable feature on this trail: about a thousand feet of hand-and-foot climbing on roots and rock in roughly half a mile, one pitch near vertical, topping out on a ridge at about 4,100 ft. If you have not used your hands, you are not on the Mildred Lakes trail. And the trail then DESCENDS off that ridge to the lakes — a trail that keeps climbing past 4,100 ft is not this one. HONEST LIMIT, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS VARIANT IS SECOND: the ground between the Mildred Lakes and Skokomish's south peak is unmaintained, brushy and easy to lose, with no marker sequence published for it. Published and trip-report accounts put the standard route on the Putvin side. Take this approach only if you have a reason to be at the Mildred Lakes, and expect to navigate rather than to follow.

climbing_route.label: Heather slopes to the 5,800-ft saddle
climbing_route.notes: From Lake of the Angels, climb westerly up pleasant alpine/heather slopes to a broad 5,800-ft saddle at the northeastern end of Mount Skokomish. Lingering steep snow and real avalanche exposure on the upper slopes persist well into summer, with hazard noted even in August/September.

climbing_route.label: Contour around the east and south flanks
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle a boot path/way-trail contours south and southwest across scree, grass, and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn.

climbing_route.label: Final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: Turn up to climb the final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge. Notoriously rotten 'Olympic choss' rock and loose scree/talus on the upper mountain and summit block are the crux of the route more than any single technical move.

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

row.overview: Mount Terror is the highest peak of the savage Southern Pickets. Its north side is the serious side: a 2,500-foot wall of rock, snow, and broken glacier ice dropping into McMillan Cirque, one of the most remote and rarely-visited big walls in the North Cascades. By contrast the south side rises only about 2,000 feet from the Crescent Creek Basin camps. This route line covers Terror's original north-side ascent line; a separate, harder and more sustained buttress (the Stoddard Buttress, 5.8) climbs the same wall further along the crest.
row.beta: Climb above the initial snowfield and make a long, ascending 3rd-class traverse rightward as the face steepens into dihedrals and cracks. Aim for the west (right) crest of the buttress about two-thirds up where the rock darkens, staying on the crest only briefly (no harder than 5.7), then move back left onto the face toward a chimney above an awkward belay — the technical crux is near the top of this chimney; some parties report a harder 5.8 traverse variant there.
row.turnaround: Given the multi-hour glacier and col crossing required just to reach the base, and the exposed, loose upper chimney, set a firm turnaround time that guarantees re-crossing the Ottohorn-Himmel col and Barrier terrain in daylight and before afternoon snow softening.
row.rappels: West Ridge notch rappels (2x ~30m) then a loose gully with several more rappels back down to Crescent Creek Cirque
row.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (this cross-country zone is walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
row.comms: Cell service is largely absent in the Terror Basin/Crescent Creek cirques, but has been reported reachable from near the summit — a call from the summit area was critical in a 2009 rescue after a rockfall accident on this face.
row.descent: Descend the West Ridge to the notch above the descent gully, then rappel and downclimb the gully into Crescent Creek Basin.
obj_haz: moat crossing at the base of the face

row.detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack (cams and stoppers to ~3in, several slings/draws) covers the technical ground; add ice axe, crampons, and glacier travel gear (rope, pickets/screws as conditions dictate) for the Ottohorn-Himmel col and Mustard Glacier crossing.
pro_tips: Study the Southern Pickets topo carefully to avoid wrong summits
row.watch_out:
Remote mountain - long approach and difficult rescue access
Mixed ice and rock climbing requiring versatile skills
Alpine terrain with weather exposure
Complex route-finding among Terror's true/false summits and neighboring Southern Pickets peaks (wrong-summit risk)
Loose rock typical of Cascade peaks
row.pro_needs: Protection is moderate for the grade — mid-size cams and stoppers protect the cracks and dihedrals on the traverse, with natural gear/slung horns useful near the crux chimney; the rock is described as generally solid but with isolated loose blocks.
row.best_season: Late July through August — enough of the season's snow has melted off the approach slabs and gullies for safe travel, while the Mustard Glacier is usually still crossable before crevasses open up too much later in the season. Earlier July trips can find firmer snow bridges but far more bugs and brush.
row.approach: From the Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead (elev. ~600 ft, reached via the unpaved Goodell Creek Road that turns north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground), follow the old abandoned roadbed/boot path northeast along Goodell Creek for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles — gentle grade, easy walking — to a stone-cairn/arrow junction near 1,700 ft marking the start of the climbers' path up toward Terror Basin. Do not continue straight past the cairn; that fainter track follows Terror Creek toward Crescent Creek Basin and is a separate (and notoriously brushier) approach. Instead take the hard right and start up the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path, which climbs directly and relentlessly through old-growth forest — roughly 3,000+ ft of gain in about 1.5 miles — before breaking out above treeline around 5,000–5,200 ft. Above the trees, a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs, and (early-season) snowfields leads to a broad saddle near 6,200 ft; the standard high camp is in a gravelly, wildflower basin about 400 ft below and beyond the saddle, around 5,800 ft, fed by several small streams (reliable water). From this Terror Basin camp, parties continue over the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin and camp again there before the climb. Hazards: the boot path itself is the crux of the approach — steep, root-and-dirt, unrelentingly brushy in places, and physically punishing (widely regarded as one of the harder approaches in the Pickets); expect loose rock and route-finding on the upper slabs approaching the saddle; if the alternate Terror Creek/Crescent Creek Basin line is used, a creek ford or logjam crossing of Terror Creek is required. Most parties treat this as a two-day approach with a high camp rather than a car-to-base push. The technical start of the North Face is reached from the Crescent Creek Basin camp by crossing the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descending the Mustard Glacier into McMillan Cirque to the foot of Terror's wall, a 2-3 hour trip even for fast parties. By mid-to-late summer the Mustard Glacier below the face is heavily crevassed with mostly unbridged, broken ice; carry glacier travel gear even though it's a small glacier.
row.descent_text: The North Face and any north-side buttress lines are steep and complex enough that essentially no one reverses them — virtually all parties, regardless of which route they climbed, descend via the West Ridge. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the West Ridge crest westward toward the low notch between Terror and The Rake, where a large chockstone marks the top of the descent gully system. From there, work down a narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully back into Crescent Creek Basin. The exact count varies with snow coverage and route-finding — figure roughly 3–5 rappels total: commonly one or two shorter raps off slung horns/chockstones or fixed pitons-and-a-nut near the ridge crest, followed by two or three more rappels down the gully itself with down-climbing in between. A single 50–60m rope is sufficient for every station reported; anchors are a mix of pre-existing fixed slings/rap rings and natural chockstone/horn anchors that may need backing up with your own gear. The gully is narrow with little shelter from rockfall, frequently has an undercut, melted-out snow moat by mid-to-late season, and the final ~100 ft is loose and marginal — expect stuck ropes in the confined terrain and manage rope ends carefully. Once down in Crescent Creek Basin, parties either regain the Barrier saddle to return to a Terror Basin camp, or exit directly via the Crescent Creek Basin/Terror Creek climbers' path, which follows the Barrier crest south before dropping to rejoin the Goodell Creek Trail for the hike out.
row.bail: Escape is difficult; the Southern Pickets are among the hardest places in the range to retreat from.

itinerary.cal: No advance permit reservation needed for this zone — pick up a walk-up wilderness permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center; best conditions are typically late July through September once Terror Creek and the approach gullies have melted out.

days.note: From the Goodell Creek Trailhead (600 ft), follow the old road bed to the cairn near 1,700 ft, then turn hard right up the steep Terror Basin climbers' path to camp in Terror Basin (about 5,800 ft). This is widely considered one of the harder approaches in the Cascades; expect route-finding and heavy brush even in good conditions.

climate.typical: Wet, maritime North Cascades climate — the Pickets sit on the range's wet west side and catch heavy Pacific moisture, so fast-moving storms and low cloud/whiteout conditions can move in with little warning even in mid-summer.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage in the Pickets is essentially absent — a signal has occasionally been found on high summits, but never count on it. This is one of the most remote and rescue-difficult areas in North Cascades NP — a satellite communicator (InReach/PLB) is strongly advised, and self-rescue should be assumed as the first line of response.
