approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Basin boot path, then over the Barrier to Crescent Creek Basin and the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the unpaved Goodell Creek Road that turns north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground, follow the old abandoned roadbed and boot path northeast along Goodell Creek for roughly 4-4.5 miles of gentle grade to a stone-cairn and arrow junction near 1,700 ft.

DO NOT CONTINUE STRAIGHT PAST THE CAIRN. That fainter track follows Terror Creek toward Crescent Creek Basin and is a separate, notoriously brushier approach. Instead take the HARD RIGHT and start up the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path, which climbs directly through old-growth forest, roughly 3,000-plus ft of gain in about 1.5 miles, before breaking out above treeline around 5,000-5,200 ft.

Above the trees a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs and early-season snowfields leads to a broad saddle near 6,200 ft; the standard high camp is in a gravelly, wildflower basin about 400 ft below and beyond the saddle, around 5,800 ft, fed by several small streams.
hazards: Committing to the wrong rib on a 2,000 ft face with limited options to reverse
A heavily crevassed, mostly unbridged Mustard Glacier below the face by mid-season
Steep, extremely loose rock near the top; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a block that had appeared solid
A narrow, rockfall-prone descent gully with an undercut melted-out moat by mid to late season
Stuck ropes in the confined descent gully, and a loose, marginal final 100 ft
Retreat from high on the route is genuinely difficult
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS JUST LEFT OF THE SNOWFIELD AT THE BOTTOM OF THE FACE, AFTER THE WALL IS ACCESSED FROM ITS WEST SIDE. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp the technical start is reached by crossing the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descending the Mustard Glacier into McMillan Cirque, then rounding into position under Terror's wall. Cross the glacier remnant beneath the face, then start JUST LEFT OF THE SNOWPATCH at the bottom.

THE MOAT WHERE SNOW MEETS ROCK AT THE BASE IS THE USUAL OBSTACLE, AND IT IS ALSO THE MARKER: you are at the base when you are standing at the gap between the snowpatch and the wall, on its left.

THE DECISION THAT DEFINES THIS ROUTE, AND IT IS MADE BEFORE THE HARD CLIMBING RATHER THAN DURING IT: THE FACE IS SPLIT BY TWO RIBS, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE RIGHT, OR WESTERN, ONE. The main risk on the lower face is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib. Long, mostly third-class pitches climb above the snowfield while TRAVERSING STEADILY RIGHTWARD; the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse. If your traverse is taking you left, you are on the wrong half of the wall.

TWO CONFIRMATIONS HIGHER, BOTH VISUAL AND BOTH USABLE IN THIN CLOUD: aim for the right or western crest of the buttress about TWO THIRDS OF THE WAY UP THE LOWER FACE, IDENTIFIABLE BY THE ROCK DARKENING. And A SHARP PROW marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Darkening rock and a sharp prow are features of this rib and not of its neighbour.

WHAT THE UPPER FACE GIVES YOU: a LONG SNOW FINGER forming a ramp that carries the route a good distance, then scrambling on a wildly exposed crest, a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits, an exposed easy-fifth hand traverse over the false summit, a downclimb, and the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top.

On the approach, when crossing from Stump Hollow into Crescent Creek Basin: DO NOT DROP INTO THE LOW NOTCH NORTH OF THE CHOPPING BLOCK. The correct line into Crescent Creek Basin is ABOUT 100 YARDS NORTH OF THAT NOTCH, AT A FLAT, BIVY-SITE SHELF ON THE RIDGE.

climbing_route.label: Glacier crossing and start of the face
climbing_route.notes: The wall is accessed from its west side after crossing the glacier remnant beneath it, and the start is just left of the snowfield at the bottom of the face. Third and fourth class scrambling on comparatively solid rock leads up to and above that snowpatch. The ice below is small but broken and mostly unbridged by mid-season, so it is treated as glacier travel; the moat where snow meets rock at the base is the usual obstacle.

climbing_route.label: Lower face rising traverse
climbing_route.notes: Long, mostly third class pitches climb above the snowfield while traversing steadily rightward. The route takes the right, or western, of the two ribs that split the north face. Parties simul-climb much of this. The main risk here is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib — the line is defined by where you exit at the top, and the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse.

climbing_route.label: Dihedrals to the buttress crest
climbing_route.notes: The ascending traverse steepens and follows dihedrals and cracks, aiming for the right or western crest of the buttress about two thirds of the way up the lower face, identifiable by the rock darkening. A sharp prow marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Time on the crest itself is brief and reported as no harder than 5.7 on generally clean, solid rock.

climbing_route.label: Chimney back on the face
climbing_route.notes: Move back left off the crest onto the face and aim for a chimney above an awkward belay. Reported difficulty here varies with the exact line: some parties keep it to about 5.4, while a variation that traverses further right lower down and takes the true buttress hits a 5.8 traverse crux near the top of the chimney. Upper pitches on this part of the wall have been described as 5.7 to 5.8 on good rock, with the original line as a whole graded III, 5.7.

climbing_route.label: Snow finger, exposed crest and the summits
climbing_route.notes: The long snow finger on the upper face forms a ramp that carries the route for a good distance; carry what you need to climb it. Above its top, the climbing turns to scrambling on a wildly exposed ridge crest, then a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits. The false summit is taken directly on an exposed easy fifth class hand traverse, then downclimbed before the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top. Rock quality deteriorates near the top, with steep, extremely loose ground reported; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a sizeable block that had appeared solid tearing loose. Descent is normally the West Ridge gully. This is one of the longest and most committing lines in the range and retreat from high on it is genuinely difficult.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out
